title: Geopolitics Energy Transition: Climate & Security Nexus | World Economic Forum
gist: Energy security, climate ambition and geopolitics (Strait of Hormuz, Ukraine) now shape one another: shocks can either accelerate renewables or entrench carbon-intensive industries. Fossil emissions are projected to fall 0.4% in 2026, but the hard work shifts to grids, supply chains, hard-to-abate sectors and pragmatic cooperation amid finance gaps.

insights.claim: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to fall 0.4% in 2026, driven by solar and wind expansion and by the conflict in Iran.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Part of the 2026 emissions decline comes from a demand/supply shock rather than structural transition, so it may not persist.
insights.quote: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026
insights.locator: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels

insights.claim: Conflicts in the Strait of Hormuz and Ukraine are disrupting energy markets and damaging energy infrastructure assets, forcing energy security, climate and geopolitics to be treated as one domain rather than separate ones.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Energy infrastructure carries rising physical geopolitical risk; price in conflict exposure when valuing assets.

insights.claim: Geopolitical shocks have a dual effect on the energy transition: they can speed diversification into renewables, but can also push countries to protect carbon-intensive incumbents in the name of energy security and self-sufficiency.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Do not assume a shock is uniformly bullish for clean energy; policy responses diverge by country.
insights.quote: geopolitical shocks can have a dual effect
insights.locator: This creates a situation in which

insights.claim: Oil markets have shown unexpected resilience and flexibility during the current shock, and unlike the 1970s oil shocks (which led to diversification, efficiency and cooperation), countries and companies may draw divergent lessons this time.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Expect fragmented policy responses rather than a coordinated efficiency/diversification wave like the 1970s.
insights.quote: Oil markets have also shown a resilience and flexibility few expected.

insights.claim: For many countries renewables are now primarily a source of low-cost domestic energy that diversifies supply, reduces exposure to international commodity markets and improves resilience, not just a climate imperative.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Renewable demand increasingly rests on security and cost motives, making it less dependent on climate policy cycles.
insights.locator: Energy security as the strongest multiplier

insights.claim: Funding renewable generation, storage and grids is framed as a long-term hedge against fuel imports whose price and availability are vulnerable to geopolitical events.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Storage and grid investment gains a security rationale, supporting sustained capex in import-dependent countries.

insights.claim: For countries without large domestic fossil fuel reserves, moving to clean energy and low-carbon production is an industrial strategy for economic independence and competitiveness, not only a climate response.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Fossil-importing economies are the most likely sustained buyers of clean-energy equipment.
insights.locator: This is where climate action and industrial strategy

insights.claim: Energy security can accelerate the transition but does not guarantee it: the Strait of Hormuz disruption strengthened the case for renewables, yet some countries may opt for energy pragmatism, including scaling domestic carbon-intensive sources.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Domestic coal/oil/gas producers may benefit from security-driven pragmatism alongside renewables.
insights.quote: Energy security can accelerate the transition – but does not guarantee it.
insights.locator: Energy security can accelerate the transition

insights.claim: Electrification across transport, buildings and industry is pushing electricity demand up faster than overall energy use, requiring major investment and upgrades in power infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Grid and power infrastructure are a structural capex beneficiary of electrification.
insights.locator: Renewable technologies have become increasingly cost-competitive

insights.claim: The critical transition challenge has shifted from deploying individual technologies to building grids, local capabilities and resilient supply chains; the WEF's Enabling the Electricity Era report calls for unlocking hidden grid capacity and delivering infrastructure faster.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: System integration (grids, supply chains) is the bottleneck where value and investment are concentrating.
insights.locator: The critical challenge is building systems

insights.claim: The harder phase of the transition lies beyond renewable power, in mobility, fertilizers, mining and heavy industry, requiring biofuels, hydrogen, carbon capture and circular-economy models rather than green electricity alone.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Hard-to-abate sector solutions are the next major investment frontier after renewable power.
insights.quote: The next major test lies beyond renewable power.
insights.locator: The next major test lies beyond renewable power

insights.claim: Emerging economies with fast-rising energy demand face a higher cost of capital than advanced economies, making cost-effective energy solutions particularly needed there.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Cost of capital, not technology, is the binding constraint for emerging-market energy build-out; blended finance is the opportunity.
insights.locator: Such a move is also a strategy

insights.claim: Climate finance, adaptation funding and loss-and-damage support continue to fall short, and the gap between Paris Agreement pledges and verifiable action has eroded trust.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Weak verification and underfunding raise policy-credibility risk for climate-linked investments.
insights.quote: the gap between climate pledges made under the Paris Agreement and verifiable action has eroded trust

insights.claim: In a fragmented geopolitical environment, cooperation is shifting from full alignment to practical, unconventional partnerships across energy, climate and national security stakeholders.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Expect deal-by-deal bilateral and minilateral energy partnerships rather than global frameworks.

insights.claim: Productive international cooperation will focus on areas of clear strategic value — resilient supply chains, grid development, technology deployment, investment, standards and capacity-building — rather than every country following the same pathway.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Supply-chain and grid projects are the likeliest to win cross-border policy support.

insights.claim: Climate policies shape industrial competitiveness while geopolitical competition shapes the availability and cost of technologies, and nature, land and biodiversity link to food systems and energy infrastructure even though governance treats them separately.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Technology costs for the transition are exposed to geopolitical competition; model trade-policy risk.
insights.locator: Energy and geopolitical shocks affect climate politics

insights.claim: The key mindset shift is that climate action is not a separate project to shield from geopolitics, and an accelerated energy transition is not a certain outcome of geopolitical events.
insights.speaker: Pim Valdre
insights.so_what: Avoid both narratives that geopolitics kills climate action and that shocks guarantee faster transition.
insights.quote: an accelerated energy transition is not a certain outcome of geopolitical events
insights.locator: The most important shift is therefore one of mindset
